newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia likely to raise taxes to counter aid cuts.
newsitem.headline: Zambia likely to raise taxes to counter aid cuts.

text.p: Zambia is likely to announce significant tax increases in 1997 to try to close the budget gap caused by a continued squeeze on aid, economic analysts said on Friday.
The government of Frederick Chiluba will be under extreme pressure to draw up a realistic budget because it lacks the assurance of normal donor inflows next year.
The donors' meeting due to start on December 12 has been deferred to February, so the January budget will be drawn up without the benefit of specific donor commitments.
Most western donors have said they will not restore aid cuts imposed this year in protest against the way the government organised general elections held on November 18.
"Zambia's budget, probably increasingly, will have to be based on domestic resources, like taxes," senior economist at the Swedish embassy in Lusaka, Robert Keller, said.
"Budgeting under uncertainty -- like uncertainty over inflows of balance of payments support -- is difficult, quite naturally," he added.
The Zambia Association of Manufacturers said it expected the government to increase its tax revenue to counter the aid cuts.
"(Increasing tax revenue) is what one would expect the government to do," association chairman Mark O'Donnell said.
He said the association expected the government to widen the tax net by, among other things, taxing the informal sector. The association would, however, reject an increase in company tax.
"They can't do that; we will not accept it. If the government did that, it would be shooting itself in the foot, because there would be no economic growth," O'Donnell said.
"We have made it clear to the government that we are not prepared for tax increases," he added.

Zambian industry is among the most heavily taxed in southern Africa, with company tax at 30 percent. Import duties range from 15 to 25 percent. Value added tax is 20 percent and income tax is 30 percent.
Finance Minister Ronald Penza hinted that government would increase its tax revenues in 1997, but declined to say how.
"We do not need the (donors') consultative group to meet before we draw up a budget. We are always looking at new strategies for raising resources," he said.
However, observers say the finance minister may be too optimistic about his ability to juggle the country's limited resources to draw up a realistic budget.
"It will be difficult for the government to sustain a budget without donor support," counsellor at the Japanese embassy Takayuki Miyashita said.
